metadata.title: Effective Teacher Policies: Insights from PISA

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD report uses PISA 2015 student assessment data and PISA teacher questionnaire data, combined with other related OECD databases, to describe and compare teacher policy features across countries and economies. The report’s Reader’s Guide indicates that country estimates and OECD averages are computed from country-level results, and that some indicators are missing when there are too few observations (e.g., fewer than 30 students or fewer than 5 schools with valid data). The excerpt provided does not specify the exact PISA sampling weight variable names (e.g., student design weights) or whether replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) were used in the statistical estimation. For analysts working with PISA microdata, the standard approach is to apply PISA complex-sample weights when producing population-representative estimates and to use the corresponding replicate method for standard errors; however, this report excerpt does not document those technical details.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a descriptive policy report synthesizing PISA 2015 results (and some comparisons across PISA 2006/2015) rather than an empirical machine-learning study that models cognitive achievement using PV-based dependent variables. The provided text does not document a specific plausible-values strategy (e.g., Rubin’s rules) for any achievement PV outcome, so PV handling cannot be verified from the excerpt. Missing data handling is also not specified beyond publication symbols and minimum observation thresholds, so the exact missing-data method for any model-based estimates is not recoverable from the provided material.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 teacher questionnaire component and PISA student assessment data for the PISA target population (15-year-olds), with country coverage reported as 72 countries and economies (35 OECD and 37 partners). The report discusses only statistically significant differences/changes and notes that some indicators are missing when there are too few observations (e.g., fewer than 30 students or fewer than 5 schools with valid data) or when data do not apply in a country. The excerpt does not provide the exact analytic inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., specific subsamples, item/module restrictions, or complete-case criteria) used for each chapter’s estimates.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report synthesizes findings from PISA 2015, including an innovation that integrates a teacher survey into the PISA assessment, and it also uses other related OECD databases and comparisons with earlier PISA cycles (notably PISA 2006). It focuses on three policy questions: (1) how high-performing systems select, develop, evaluate and compensate teachers; (2) how teacher sorting across schools relates to equity; and (3) how countries attract and retain people into teaching. The report provides cross-country descriptive comparisons and discusses statistically significant differences/changes, while noting that some indicators are missing when there are too few observations or when data do not apply. It reports several benchmark-style results such as the share of disadvantaged schools receiving smaller classes and/or lower student-teacher ratios, the inequitable distribution of teacher qualifications/experience, and the proportion of 15-year-olds expecting to work as teachers. The excerpt does not provide the technical estimation details (e.g., PV combination rules, exact missing-data method, or weighting variable names), so causal interpretation is limited and the statistical mechanics of the estimates cannot be fully audited from the provided text.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is extracted from an OECD policy report rather than an empirical ML paper with a documented predictive pipeline. The excerpt does not provide an analytic sample size, per-country student counts, or any machine-learning model training/evaluation procedure; therefore, fields such as total_students, per-country n_students, and ML technique lists cannot be populated from the provided text. The report’s findings are presented as descriptive and comparative policy insights from PISA and related datasets, so the schema’s ML-specific outputs (main_findings as predictive targets) are intentionally left empty.
